notes:
I covered all 25 verses, but not every source type you asked for. I didn't find any Catholic, Orthodox, Bible Odyssey, NET notes, Wesley-on-Judges-21 or prosperity/word-of-faith material, so those are left out. The Protestant disagreements I found are between individual teachers rather than clearly along denominational lines. I've noted the teacher's tradition where it's known.

**Overview**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) sums up the chapter this way: Israel refused to simply repent and break its oath, and instead turned to worse fixes. These were wiping out Jabesh-gilead and then a scheme for Benjamite men to "kidnap" women at a feast. [source] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-21/
- Dale Ralph Davis (quoted by Constable) says the writer reports events but hardly comments, so readers must work out how to take the story. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html

**v. 1**
- Guzik: given their anger, the oath probably seemed right, but it had consequences they didn't foresee. Justice also guards against punishment that is too harsh. [source] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-21/
- Matthew Henry: God's law forbade marrying Canaanites, and forcing that would in effect send Benjamin off to serve other gods. So where could wives come from? [source] https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_021.cfm
- Constable: the oath may echo Deuteronomy 7:1-3 (no marrying Canaanites), but that rule was for Canaanites, not fellow Israelites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html
- Precept Austin compares it to Jephthah's rash vow. Both lead to tragedy for young women, and Jephthah's daughter's dance even mirrors the Shiloh dances. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_21_commentary

**v. 2**
- Coffman: this happened soon after the war, while the ark was still at Bethel and before it moved to Shiloh. [source] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/judges-21.html
- Precept Austin: they wept because they had acted hastily without seeking God's will. [source] https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_21_commentary

**v. 3**
- Constable: they asked God to explain, but the real cause was their own failure to seek Him earlier. He sees no mourning over sin and no turning back to the Lord. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html
- Gaebelein: the answer to "why?" was their sin and departure from God, and people today likewise blame God for war instead of sin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_21_commentary

**v. 4**
- Constable: an altar is odd here, since they had just sacrificed at Bethel (20:26). They may have rebuilt, enlarged or added one. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html
- Precept Austin: puzzling that they made offerings yet never asked God for direction, for example through Phinehas. [source] https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_21_commentary

**v. 5**
- Keil & Delitzsch: the assembly could rightly threaten no-shows with death. But only the truly guilty could be punished, not women and children unless they too had earned death. [source] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/21-25.htm
- Constable: the "great oath" probably meant that tribes skipping the nation's battles faced punishment (compare Numbers 32:20-33). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html

**vv. 6–7**
- Precept Austin: Israel was "reaping the rotten fruit" of doing what was right in its own eyes. [source] https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_21_commentary
- Constable: they should have admitted the oath was a mistake and asked for God's solution. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html

**vv. 8–9**
- Hawker (Anglican): the attack seems aimed more at getting wives for Benjamin than at punishing Jabesh-gilead's absence. [source] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pmc/judges-21.html
- Constable: Jabesh-gilead lay about 48 miles northeast of Shiloh, east of the Jordan. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html

**v. 10**
- Precept Austin: they fixed the near-loss of one tribe by killing more Israelites. [source] https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_21_commentary
- Constable calls it a sinful plan driven by self-will and revenge. He also quotes Cundall: it looks extremely cruel today, but the near-sacred bond between the tribes must be appreciated. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html

**v. 11**
- Treasury of Scripture Knowledge (via Precept Austin): this copies the orders against Midian in Numbers 31:17-18, which Israel apparently took as a precedent. [source] https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60766/
- Precept Austin: the Hebrew "devote to destruction" was elsewhere aimed at pagan peoples, never a tribe of Israel. Nothing suggests God backed this. [source] https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_21_commentary

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: "in the land of Canaan" also appears in Joshua 21:2 and 22:9. He wonders whether there was another Shiloh east of the Jordan. [source] https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/21-12.html
- Henry: the Jabesh fathers never took the oath, and war captives belonged to the victors. He suggests this tie explains why Saul, a Benjamite, later cared about Jabesh (1 Samuel 11). [source] https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_021.cfm

**v. 13**
- Precept Austin: literally "called peace to them," the same idiom as Deuteronomy 20:10. [source] https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_21_commentary

**v. 14**
- Precept Austin: surprising that the Benjamites trusted the other tribes, though the offer of wives "sweetened the deal." [source] https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_21_commentary
- Guzik: one wrong done to fix another. Israel should have renounced the oath and given its own daughters. [source] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-21/
- Constable: that the plan fell short shows it wasn't God's will, though He allowed it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html

**v. 15**
- Constable: the Lord made the gap only in the sense that He allowed it. He would not let Benjamin vanish, because of His promises. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html
- Kretzmann (Lutheran) reads "repented" as anxious concern over the near-loss of a tribe. [source] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/judges-21.html

**v. 16**
- Precept Austin: they still haven't asked God. It's "what shall *we* do," not what God might do. [source] https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_21_commentary

**v. 17**
- Keil & Delitzsch: Benjamin's land must stay an independent holding for the survivors, so they needed wives. [source] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/judges-21.html

**v. 18**
- Precept Austin: this is the third mention of the oath. Confessing the foolish oath would have been better than this "charade." [source] https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60766/

**v. 19**
- Constable lists three views of the feast: Passover (Keil & Delitzsch, linking the dances to Miriam's), Tabernacles at grape harvest (Cundall), or a festival Israel made up (Block). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html
- Coffman: it was one of Israel's three yearly feasts at the central shrine. [source] https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/21-21.html

**vv. 20–21** (the main disagreement among teachers)
- Guzik: a "little drama" of "kidnapping," with women he calls "no doubt willing," so the marriages could happen without official approval. [source] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-21/
- Constable takes the opposite view: the plan required kidnapping and raping 200 women. It kept the letter of the oath but broke a more basic law. [source] https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/21-21.html
- Henry (Presbyterian nonconformist) calls it a "preposterous way of match-making" that must never be treated as a precedent. [source] https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_021.cfm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: dance was part of worship, done outdoors with the women apart. They compare the scheme to the Romans' seizing of the Sabine women. [source] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/21-25.htm
- Gill (Baptist): each man was to take only one wife. [source] https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/21-21.html
- Hawker uses it to warn against worldly dancing and revelry. [source] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pmc/judges-21.html

**v. 22**
- Kretzmann paraphrases the elders' reply: the women weren't taken as war booty, as at Jabesh, but in peace. Since the fathers didn't give them, they bear no guilt. [source] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/judges-21.html
- Constable: the fathers would complain about how the women were treated and about losing the usual bride-price. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html
- Ligonier (Reformed) calls this the reasoning of "twisted minds." [source] https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/wives-benjamin

**v. 23**
- Keil & Delitzsch: 200 wives, and they rebuilt towns that had been burned. [source] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/judges-21.html
- BibleHub's commentary: Scripture records this without approving every detail. [source] https://biblehub.com/judges/21-23.htm
- Henry/Coffman: the women married men who now held the whole tribe's estates. [source] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/judges-21.html

**v. 24**
- Keil & Delitzsch: the assembly's representatives split up and went home. [source] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/21-25.htm

**v. 25**
- Keil & Delitzsch: implies such things couldn't have happened under a just king. [source] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/21-25.htm
- Gill: the events of chapters 17–21 fall between Joshua's death and the first judges. His list of evils includes Israel's harshness to Benjamin, the slaughter at Jabesh-gilead and the "rape of the daughters of Shiloh." [source] https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/jps/judges/21-25.html
- Ligonier: moral and theological anarchy that only a righteous king could solve. [source] https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/wives-benjamin
- Clarke: the writer reports these atrocities but doesn't justify them. [source] https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/21-25.html
- Cambridge Bible: a fitting transition to Samuel and the start of the monarchy. [source] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/21-25.htm

**Other views** (only what's quoted in the evangelical sources above)
- Constable quotes Trible: "The rape of one has become the rape of six hundred." He also quotes Olson: sticking to the technical wording of rules while ignoring love and faithfulness leads to disaster. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html
- Constable also quotes Merrill: the story reflects badly on Benjamin and Saul's family line and is clearly pro-David. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-21.html
